---
title: "A figure that carries its own provenance"
description: "plot_manifest() fingerprints a plot's data, spec, and resolved fonts; plot_svg(manifest = TRUE) embeds that in the file; plot_verify() checks a figure still matches its data — and tells a font difference apart from a data change."
categories: [Backend]
image: figs/provenance.png
---



Six months after a report ships, somebody asks whether figure 3 was made from the
data currently in the repository. Usually there is no way to answer that except to
re-run the script and compare images by eye — which fails for reasons that have
nothing to do with the data, because the machine has a different font stack now.

Since a vellumplot plot is a spec rather than a picture, it can be fingerprinted
before it is drawn.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p <- vplot(mtcars, width = 6.5, height = 4) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp, size = 2.2) |>
  mark_smooth(x = wt, y = mpg, method = "lm", se = TRUE) |>
  scale_color_continuous() |>
  labs(title = "Weight against mileage", x = "weight (1000 lbs)", y = "mpg",
       color = "hp")
```
:::



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figs/provenance.png){width=100%}
:::
:::


`plot_manifest()` returns that fingerprint: a hash of the input data (sensitive to
row order and columns), the data's shape, a structural hash of the spec, how many
elements the plot emits, and the font faces it actually resolved to.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m <- plot_manifest(p)
m$data$hash
#> [1] "33f1aa2876d0ad2a1232bcd25a9a350e"
m$spec_hash
#> [1] "f830124ff2425cd2f2e7b97f00ec96ea"
m$n_elements
#> [1] 24
```
:::


The fonts are the part that is easy to overlook and the part that makes the check
usable:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
str(m$fonts, max.level = 2, list.len = 2)
#> 'data.frame':	1 obs. of  3 variables:
#>  $ path  : chr "/System/Library/Fonts/Helvetica.ttc"
#>  $ index : int 0
#>   [list output truncated]
```
:::


## Embedding it in the file

`plot_svg(manifest = TRUE)` writes the SVG with the manifest inside it, so the
figure travels with its own provenance. `plot_verify()` reads it back and
recomputes the data hash:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
svg <- plot_svg(p, manifest = TRUE)
check <- plot_verify(svg, mtcars)
check$ok
#> [1] TRUE
```
:::


Hand it different data and it says so — and says *which* thing changed:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tampered <- mtcars
tampered$mpg[1] <- tampered$mpg[1] + 1

bad <- plot_verify(svg, tampered)
c(ok = bad$ok, data_ok = bad$data_ok, fonts_ok = bad$fonts_ok)
#>       ok  data_ok fonts_ok 
#>    FALSE    FALSE     TRUE
```
:::


That split is the point. `data_ok` is whether the data still hashes the same;
`fonts_ok` is whether every font the figure was drawn with is still on this
machine. A pixel difference with `data_ok = TRUE` and `fonts_ok = FALSE` is the
font stack, not your analysis — a different cause with a different fix (install the
font) than a changed dataset. Reporting them together as "the figure does not
match" is what makes reproducibility checks so easy to ignore.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bad$expected
#> [1] "33f1aa2876d0ad2a1232bcd25a9a350e"
bad$actual
#> [1] "00a30c3af8e14eab951e12fffb03eab4"
```
:::


## The scene is a value too

One layer down, the same idea applies to the scene rather than the plot.
`vellum::scene_hash()` and `scene_diff()` compare two scenes structurally — what
changed, not which pixels — which is a better regression test than an image diff,
because it does not care what the font stack looks like on the machine running the
test.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(vellum)
a <- vl_scene(4, 2, bg = "white") |>
  draw(circle_grob(x = 0.4, y = 0.5, r = 0.2, gp = vl_gpar(fill = "#c9a874"),
                   name = "blob"))
b <- vl_scene(4, 2, bg = "white") |>
  draw(circle_grob(x = 0.4, y = 0.5, r = 0.2, gp = vl_gpar(fill = "#c1121f"),
                   name = "blob"))

scene_hash(a) == scene_hash(b)
#> [1] FALSE
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
scene_diff(a, b)
#> 1 difference:
#> • ~ root$children[1]$gp$fill: #c9a874 -> #c1121f
```
:::


Both of these are checks you can put in a test suite and have them mean something
in CI, where there is no display, no fonts you chose, and no human to look at the
picture. See also [One scene, three formats](three-formats.qmd) for why the same
solved scene is what every backend walks.
